blocks.content: The texture of an igneous rock is primarily determined by the rate at which the magma or lava cools and crystallizes.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The rate of cooling of magma or lava is the primary factor controlling the crystal size and overall texture of igneous rocks.
Phaneritic texture consists of coarse grains visible to the naked eye, indicating slow cooling deep underground within plutonic bodies.
Aphanitic texture features fine-grained crystals that require magnification, resulting from rapid cooling at or near the Earth's surface.
Porphyritic texture reflects a two-stage cooling history, characterized by large phenocrysts embedded within a finer groundmass.
Vesicular texture arises when expanding gas bubbles become trapped in solidifying lava, producing cavities called vesicles.
Direct correlation between cooling rates and grain size is a high-yield topic: slow intrusive cooling produces coarse grain, while fast extrusive cooling produces fine grain.
Questions frequently test the distinction between phenocrysts (large crystals) and matrix/groundmass in porphyritic rocks to infer a two-stage cooling history.
Be prepared to identify obsidian (glassy) and pumice (vesicular) based on their specific physical formation conditions rather than mineral composition alone.
